newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails U.S. deficit fall to $37 billion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails U.S. deficit fall to $37 billion.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday announced a dramatic fall in the projected U.S. budget deficit this fiscal year and said he would use a new authority to strike some wasteful spending from the budget.

Speaking at a White House news conference that ranged from budget details to campaign finance reform and the Middle East, Clinton began by hailing a fall in the budget deficit estimate to just $37 billion in the year to October.
Clinton predicted a balanced budget agreement with Congress signed into law on Tuesday would break a cycle of federal deficits dating to 1969 and would actually produce budget surpluses soon.

"With our bipartisan balanced budget plan, we now expect it not only to reach balance by 2002, but to have a surplus in excess of $20 billion, and to be able to maintain that for several years thereafter," he said.

Assessing the budget and tax bills he signed during an elaborate ceremony at the White House on Tuesday, Clinton said he expected he would use his line-item veto authority to root out cases of wasteful spending.
"The short answer is there will be some exercise of that," Clinton said, referring to new authority he has to strip items from spending and tax measures without vetoing an entire bill.
Under the law, which went into effect this year but has yet to be used, a president has five days to veto portions of legislation he deems to be unfairly caring for the needs of special interests.
The White House is reviewing 79 tax breaks for specific companies and individuals that were included in the budget plan. Clinton has until Monday to act on those.

Clinton, defending the overall package from critics who question whether it was necessary to close the ever-narrowing deficit, said the spending gap would have mushroomed next year without the measures.

"We now expect the deficit to drop to $37 billion," he said. "Yet without the bipartisan balanced budget we just passed, my budget officials estimate the deficit would rise next year to $50 to $100 billion and stay at that level for years to come."
The revised estimate for the current fiscal year, which ends September 30, is dramatically below last year's deficit figure of $107 billion.

Separately, the Congressional Budget Office announced on Wednesday it was projecting an even lower fiscal 1997 deficit than the White House. It said the amount of government red ink this fiscal year would be the lowest since 1974 at just $34 billion.
Discussing other subjects during his lengthy exchange with reporters, his 15th formal news conference this year, Clinton:
-- Said the Middle East peace process could not proceed unless Israel was convinced the Palestinian Authority was doing all it could to maintain security in the region.

"Until the parties trust each other and until the Israelis believe that the Palestinian Authority is making 100 percent effort, which is different from 100 percent results ... it is impossible for peace to proceed," he said.
-- Stressed that under the law he can only intervene in the Teamsters union strike against United Parcel Service if there was a threat of "severe damage" to the economy.
Restrictions are "very high before the president can intervene," he said.
-- Clinton refused to apologise for his continued fund-raising activities on behalf of the Democratic Party, even though he says the so-called "soft money" he raises should be banned.
"I plead guilty to that," he said of raising money. "I don't believe in unilateral disarmament." He insisted it would be "a grave mistake for us to abandon any attempt to compete" with Republicans.
